study.title: Psalm 73 The crisis of the prosperity of the wicked and the good of approaching God
study.overview: This psalm of Asaph describes a real spiritual struggle: the psalmist begins by stating that God is good for his people, but confesses that he almost stumbled by envying the prosperity of the wicked. In observing the apparent tranquility of the wicked, their arrogance and the immediate absence of judgment, he was tempted to think that fidelity was useless. The turn happens when he enters the sanctuary of God and begins to see the end of these people in the light of the divine presence. The psalm ends with a mature confession: the greatest good is not in earthly prosperity, but in being close to God, trusting in him and proclaiming his works.

outline.title: The Goodness of God and the Properness of the Perverses
outline.explanation: The psalmist opens with a central truth: God is good for Israel, especially for those with a clean heart. But he soon admits that he almost lost his spiritual balance by comparing his life with that of the arrogant. He sees the wicked prospering, without apparent pains, full of pride, violence and blasphemy, as if nothing reached them.

outline.title: The inner temptation and the turn of the sanctuary
outline.explanation: Faced with this apparent injustice, the psalmist even think that keeping the heart clean was useless. He also realizes that speaking in this way could scandalize the people of God. The crisis remains until he enters the sanctuaries of God; there he gains a new perspective and understands the final destiny of the wicked.

outline.title: The end of the arrogant and the confession of ignorance
outline.explanation: In the presence of God, the psalmist understands that the prosperity of the wicked is fragile and passing. Their judgment may seem sudden, like a dream that disappears when awakening. He then recognizes that his bitterness led him to act as foolish and to speak as who does not understand the reality of God.

outline.title: The safety of being near God
outline.explanation: After inner correction, the psalmist affirms the continuous company of God, his direction and his future hope of being received in glory. He concludes that God is superior to any good in heaven or on earth, the strength of his heart and his eternal portion. The closeness of God is declared as the true good, together with the trust and testimony of the divine works.

study.context: The text itself and notes present the psalm as a song of Assafe, an integral part of the third part of the psaltery. Tyndale's note notes that the psalm deals with the apparent prosperity of the wicked and the crisis that this causes in the faith of the psalmist. Notes also indicate that the "sanctuary" is the place where it receives a new view of reality. There is no secure base for additional date details, specific historical occasion or location beyond what the text suggests in the notes.
study.theology: The psalm confronts one of the greatest tensions of the life of faith: God is good, but the world often seems to reward wickedness. The biblical answer is not to deny the difficulty, but to lead the crisis to the presence of God. The prosperity of the wicked is shown as temporary and deceptive, while communion with God is permanent and sufficient. Divine justice may not be immediate in human eyes, but the psalm states that the end of the wicked is in the hands of the Lord. There is also a theology of perseverance: God holds the believer's hand, guides by his counsel and receives his people in glory. True wealth is not material, but God Himself as a portion, rock and supreme of the heart.

scholarViews.insight: The psalm is a psalm of wisdom that investigates the apparent injustice of the prosperity of the wicked and shows that God's presence in the sanctuary gives the psalmist a perspective that goes beyond the present life.
The psalmist was tempted to think that he had purified his heart in vain, but restrained the word not to scandalize the generation of the children of God.
Entering the sanctuary corrects the false conclusions of the psalmist and shows him the dark reverse of the state of the wicked who once seemed prosperous.

questions: When I see ungodly prospering people, is my first reaction envy or seeking God's presence?
What truths of the psalm can prevent me from concluding that fidelity to God is useless?
How can trust in the Lord change my way of measuring success, safety and future?
study.practice: In facing comparisons and frustrations, take the crisis to God before turning doubt into a bitter word. Set up time for worship, prayer and sincere examination, asking the Lord to adjust his vision. Remember daily that the closeness of God is worth more than quick gains, and practice gratitude for his direction, care and presence. It is also worth witnessing with simplicity: tell the works of God rather than feeding the complaint against his righteousness.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not allow to safely define the exact historical context of the psalm, nor to affirm details about author, date or original situation beyond the assignment to Asasafe. In 73:10, textual tradition and translations vary widely, and the exact meaning of the phrase is uncertain; therefore, the reading here accompanies the general flow of the text and notes, without treating a single translation as definitive.
